function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run inside a script) to finish the whole workflow locally.  
I’ll also give you the exact files you need to create/modify so that you can commit them and push to the remote repo yourself.

> **NOTE** – I don’t have network access from here, so I can’t actually clone or push to GitHub.  
> The instructions below assume you have `git`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and `yq` (or any YAML editor) installed on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick scan to see what the project contains:

```bash
tree -L 2
```

Typical output (you may see something like):

```
├── app.js
├── package.json
├── README.md
└── .gitignore
```

* `app.js` – the entry point of the Node.js app  
* `package.json` – dependencies and scripts  
* No existing Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, or GitHub Actions workflow.

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```Dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
LABEL description="Node.js welcome app"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and stable.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs.  
> * Exposes port `3000` (adjust if your app uses a different port).  
> * Uses `node app.js` as the entrypoint – matches the typical Node pattern.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAML files

Create a directory `k8s` (or place the files directly in the repo root) and add two files:

#### `deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### `service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Tip:** If you want external access, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`.

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Uncomment and configure if you want to deploy automatically
      # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
      # with:
      #   manifests: k8s/*.yaml
      #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **What this does**  
> * Builds the Docker image on every push to `main`.  
> * Pushes it to Docker Hub (you’ll need to set `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` in the repo’s Secrets).  
> * Optionally deploys to a Kubernetes cluster if you enable the commented section and add a `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` secret.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new/modified files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you created the `k8s` folder directly in the repo root, adjust the path accordingly.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit and push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## Quick sanity check

After pushing, verify that:

1. The GitHub Actions tab shows a successful run.  
2. The Docker image appears in Docker Hub under `zelarhq/nodejs-welcome`.  
3. You can apply the Kubernetes manifests:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
```

…and then check the pod status:

```bash
kubectl get pods
kubectl get svc
```

---

### Recap of the files you added/updated

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Container image definition |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment spec |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Service spec |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline |

Feel free to tweak the image tags, replica counts, or service type to match your production needs. Happy coding!
